questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the key mistake in treating 'governance documentation' as a single policy file?
options: A working governance program actually needs several distinct kinds of documentation, each serving a different audience and updated on a different rhythm
There is no mistake -- one file is always sufficient
Governance documentation should never be written down at all
Only the data dictionary needs to exist; every other document is optional
questions.explain: The lesson lists five distinct documentation types (charter, standards, data dictionary, ADRs, release records), each with its own audience and update rhythm -- not one catch-all file.

questions.q: What does an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) primarily capture, per this lesson?
options: Only the final decision, with no explanation needed
What was decided, what alternatives were seriously considered, and why this option was chosen over the others, written at the time the decision was made
A complete technical specification of every field in an object
A log of every user login for the past year
questions.explain: An ADR's core value is the reasoning -- the why -- captured at decision time, not just a record of what was ultimately built, which can usually be seen by looking at the org anyway.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the 'why' behind a decision is harder to recover later than the 'what'?
options: Because the 'what' is always classified and inaccessible
Because the 'why' is always identical to the 'what' in practice
Because Salesforce automatically deletes all reasoning after one year
Because what was built can usually be seen by examining the org, but the reasoning behind choosing that approach over alternatives is lost unless it was written down at the time
questions.explain: The lesson explains that an architect can inspect the org to see what was built, but the reasoning for choosing it over the alternatives disappears unless an ADR recorded it at the time.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why can stale documentation be worse than having no documentation at all?
options: Stale documentation is never actually trusted by anyone, so it causes no harm
Stale documentation is a criminal offense under data protection law
Stale documentation looks authoritative and is trusted, but is wrong -- leading to decisions made on incorrect information, which is worse than knowing you need to verify firsthand
There is no meaningful difference between stale and current documentation
questions.explain: The danger the lesson describes is specifically that stale documentation still looks trustworthy, so people rely on it without verifying -- unlike having no documentation, where the need to verify is at least obvious.

questions.q: How does this lesson say documentation ownership should be assigned?
options: Mapped to specific roles -- e.g., the change owner updates the data dictionary as part of submitting a change, the architect writes ADRs, and the CoE owns the charter and standards
As a vague 'everyone's responsibility,' which in practice ensures it gets done consistently
Only the CEO is allowed to update any governance document
Documentation should never have a named owner, to avoid bureaucracy
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly rejects 'everyone's responsibility' as meaning nobody's, and ties ownership to the specific roles introduced in Lesson 9.
